by: referee for the VERDICT review's proposed re-rulings (closure pass, 2026-11-10)
about: Rulings on the eight items of VERDICT section 10's re-rule table and the recheck's notes. Each entry lists every judged row it touches. 'accept' entries change the settled cells when this file is renamed to rerulings.cells.json; 'reject' entries keep the settled cell (from equals to) and say why. A null in 'to' means the cell loses that field. RR-12 to RR-19 rule on items 1 to 7 of VERDICT draft 3's section 11.3 (2026-11-11); an entry whose 'rows' is empty touches closure rows only, named in 'closure_rows'.

cells.why: The fail called E-13 a measured ceiling. It is not one, so the cell is open as worded. (1) E-13 reads its own result as 'met at the median on this disk and not at the tail': the group's longest gap was 9.8 and 9.7 ms at the median of 15 handovers, against 10 ms. (2) The 24.4 and 30.8 ms worst cases are the longest gap between any two acks in a window from 0.2 s before to 3 s after the handover. The same measure over a quiet window with no handover reached 22.9 ms (4.4 to 22.9), and E-01 found 22 to 52 ms flush stalls in every fio run. So the tail is this disk's stalls; the handover itself adds about 4 ms, and the first new write after it was acked in 2.0 and 2.5 ms at the median (1.0 to 6.7). (3) The numbers are etcd's Go server. A port runs the same steps (a vote, an fsync, a commit), so etcd's figure bounds nothing for it the way E-02's pipeline bounds a kernel. (4) The native bar of 2 ms names NVMe, which this box lacks; judge 2's own native reason says 'the gap is this disk's'. (5) AMENDMENTS 1.3, the line both judges cite, ends 'or it stays open'. The failover clause is open in both readings (E + 0.25 E sums to 2.5 s, reasoned, not run), and the writes etcd drops in a transfer are A-02's refuse-at-once rule, which every Raft row takes. So as worded the cell equals the restated one: open, with no alternative, no dependence and no gap. Its closer stays: pins on three processes of the port with A-02's constants and the refuse-at-once handover.

The fail called E-08's p99 a ceiling. It is one working point, so as worded the cell is open. E-08 measured p99 1.2 ms (Node) and 3.5 ms (Rust) 'at a load where each relay used about half a core' (1,723 and 3,337 records a second, 1,000 subscribers in 64 rooms). Its own sweep shows the latency follows the load: one probe at 0.38 of a core gave p99 0.79 ms, under the bar of about 0.83 ms, while the three timed runs at the same rate gave 1.0 to 1.4 ms. Rust being slower than Node at equal load shows the build set the number, not the language or the protocol, and E-08 calls the result a latency budget. P-05 names no load and no socket count, so no measured point bounds every load. The bar is likely missed above light load; it is not shown missed by design. The restated cells do not move: met for these rows (a window per room and about 1,000 sockets a core; E-22, E-31, E-08). OBJ and V4 are not touched: they fail as worded on their own reasons too (OBJ's commit is a PUT at 2.67 ms p99, E-28; V4 has no one order per room).
evidence: experiments/E08-relay-fanout/README.md (the half-CPU rows and the sweep table)

cells.why: The same reason as RR-02: E-08's 1.2 ms is one prototype's working point at about half a core, not a ceiling, and P-05 names no load. As worded these rows are open, the same as restated, so the cell loses its alternative, its dependence and its gap. BUY: judge 2 also cited JetStream's 1.31 ms p99 ack with fsync on three replicas (E-09b). That is a fail only if a room message must be `persisted`, which P-05 does not say; at its default JetStream acks one publisher at 0.55 ms p99 (E-09b). So it does not prove the fail either.

The fail stands; its reason and gap change. Old reason: 'C = 0.73 ms is the floor of any persisted commit'. C is a sum of two p99s (three-writer fsync 676 us plus round trip 58 us), not a floor: a commit needs only the second-fastest of three fsyncs (VERDICT section 1 says so too). New reason, PERF-01's own win rule: a win needs fero's median better than JetStream's by more than the larger spread. JetStream's default one-publisher p99 was 0.550 ms over runs of 0.536 to 0.783 ms (E-09b), so a win needs a p99 below about 0.30 ms. The best a `persisted` commit can do here: the second-fastest of the leader's fsync and two followers' fsync plus a round trip, sampled from E-01's one-writer fdatasync table (290,235 samples), with independent disks, has p99 0.364 ms; with the client's hop, 0.422 ms. The evidence skeptic, the recheck (V-17) and this referee each computed it; it has no CPU, batching or forwarding cost, so a real kernel can only approach it (rule 1's ceiling, as E-02's pipeline). On this box's one shared disk a real commit is slower still. So these rows, whose only durable rung is `persisted`, cannot win the default row, and PERF-01 allows no loss today. Gap: (0.422 - 0.303) / 0.303 = 0.39. That is the distance the proof shows. A gap counted from C (1.41) would count from a sum the study itself says is not this row's floor, so it would claim more than is shown. The alternative and its dependence stay: if the user accepts this row as a loss by name (PERF-01, VERDICT item 2), the cell is open. Basis: reasoned from measured parts.
evidence: VERDICT.review.json: skeptic evidence S1; recheck V-17

cells.why: Both judges scored met on E-20's model. E-20 has no lock token. E-32's crossing model put E-20's dedup beside E-17's lock-token refusal and found, in 6 steps, a write both applied and told 'refused': the refusal judged a late copy whose outcome the dedup floor had already forgotten. The fix (the floor guards the refusal path, `refuse.above`) was model-checked only with D `sess`. E-32 says of them: 'not checked here, and owed the same floor rule by reasoning'. So the path that broke is in these rows and is not shown safe in a model of their own dedup. By the referee's own F-02 rulings for SLOG, OBJ, ISR and SIDE, a row's own rule must be shown before it is met. Not fails: the fix is small, has a precedent (Raft thesis 6.3) and no model of these rows breaks with it. Closer: E-32's `floor-*` bounds run with D `win` and the floor on the refusal path. The `sess` rows keep met: the counterexample needs no move and no healing, and E-32 checked the fix with `sess`. SLOG is already open.

Kept open in both readings. A structural fail needs PD's own shape to miss $10 whatever the machine count. cells.why: Kept open. Both judges wrote 'data is not the engine on PD's servers' and still scored open, on purpose: PD 'meets DATA-01 only if a differential test proves that store's rows equal data's fold'. That path is in the requirements: DATA-09 says that if any layer moves to native code, 'the fold's results stay data's, proven by a differential test against data'. AMENDMENTS A-30 names PD (by reasoning) and SRV as the rows that fold natively and take that test. The proposed argument, 'a differential test cannot show that data's lane folds', reads DATA-01 without DATA-09. Read that way it fails SRV by the same steps (its servers fold plain rows in Rust or Go), yet only PD was proposed. No step shows PD's rows cannot equal data's fold: under Percolator's locks the commits on one key land in one order, and MVCC picks no winner between concurrent writes, so there is no last-writer-wins compare to point at (reasoned). No second agent confirmed the argument in writing. Whether a server may fold natively at all is a reading of the user's own two requirements; it is listed as a user choice. Closer unchanged: DATA-09's differential test of the server's fold, 1e6 records.

cells.by: referee for the closure pass's family B leads (2026-11-11)
cells.why: Open, not met. These four rows hold Q `mix`, so they carry the `memory` rung (the settled memory-rung unit: DRAFT, CELL, SPLIT, COMP). A `memory` write commits when a majority holds it in memory, and the disks catch up within about a second. If a majority of that group stops uncleanly inside that second, the write is gone: DESIGN-V5 decision 4b says such a stop 'needs `fero recover`', which only lists what may be lost (F-12). A `persisted` write survives 'a power loss of all of them' (DESIGN-V5 3.2); a `memory` write does not. The family B referee's trace for two-phase commit (B1, B3) works the same way for a saga. Checked here against the saga's own rules (E-24's `fullundo`, A-24): (1) a unit has a step on p, a `memory` resource, and a step on q, a `persisted` one; (2) both steps commit, and the holder records the unit `done` in #sagas; (3) a majority of p's group stops uncleanly inside the window, and its replicas come back as new. Now q keeps its step and p has lost its own, while #sagas says `done`, so no later holder takes the unit up again. That is half a unit, which P-15 forbids: 'every unit ends all applied or all undone' (its acceptance test; E-24's property A1). A second path breaks the paused-holder clause. The ender's last write at p also raised p's fence (that is why `fullundo` works in E-24), and that raise sits in the lost tail. E-24 says of unclean recovery that 'a fence table can go back', so a paused holder's late step with its old token can land at p after the unit ended: E-24's 12-step case comes back. E-24 is the only support for the met cell, and it leaves unclean recovery out in its own words. AMENDMENTS 4 lists this very crossing as open for COMP (K-09: the unsynced tail and what it held, 'lock fence tokens' among them), and G-05 says the rung's safety was never modelled. So 'met' has no support for these rows. Not fails. The trace is reasoned, not run or model-checked, and no second agent confirmed a structural argument (rule 1). One stated rule inside the row closes it: a saga's steps, fence raises and end record on a `memory` resource commit at `persisted` (Q `mix` may choose per write), or the saga library refuses such a unit. No row states that rule. This is the verdict the family B referee gave B1 and B3 for the same trace, with no alternative and no dependence. The saga rows with Q `maj-d` keep met: there a committed step is lost only when a majority's disks are lost for good, F-12's operator case, which no row's P-15 cell counts. P-15 (S) does not move: it is already 'not' for every saga row (a saga shows its steps one at a time). Closer: E-24's saga model with a group that can lose its unsynced tail when a majority stops uncleanly, once without the rule (it should break A1) and once with it.
evidence: E-24 (experiments/E24-sagas-ramp/README.md: property A1, the `fullundo` option, 'What the models leave out': unclean recovery)

cells.by: referee for VERDICT draft 3's re-rule list (VERDICT.md section 11.3, items 1 to 7), 2026-11-11
cells.why: Open, not met, for RR-11's reason. These four rows carry the `memory` rung (Q `mix`), and no rule of theirs keeps a lock's protected writes off a `memory` resource. If a majority of that group stops uncleanly inside the sync window, the tail it acknowledged is gone, and the writer's fence table goes back with it. The trace, by the rows' own rules: (1) holder A takes lock L with token t1 and pauses; (2) L lapses, holder B takes it with token t2 and writes to p, a `memory` resource; p's leader raises its fence for L to t2 and acknowledges; (3) a majority of p's group stops uncleanly before its disks catch up, its replicas come back as new, and `fero recover --unclean` rebuilds the group from what is left, without B's write and without the raise; (4) A wakes and writes to p under t1, and p's table now holds t1 or less, so the write commits. A write under t1 has committed after a write under t2 was acknowledged. TEST-13's fencing checker fails that history, and P-10 says 'a write with an older token than one a writer has seen is refused'. The recovery bumps the epochs of p's slots (DESIGN-V5 4.2), but a token is a version of `#locks`' own slot, so the bump does not reach it: tokens still rise, while p's record of the highest one it saw goes back. The met cell's support never loses an acknowledged tail: E-22's lock check, E-21, E-17 and E-33 keep every committed entry, and E-24 says of unclean recovery that 'a fence table can go back'. AMENDMENTS 4 lists 'lock fence tokens' in K-09's unsynced tail, and G-05 says the rung's safety was never modelled. So 'met' has no support for these rows. Not fails: the trace is reasoned, not run or model-checked, no second agent has confirmed it in writing, and one stated rule closes it. Closer: either no protected write, fence raise or saga record sits on a `memory` resource (the refusal of RR-14), or `fero recover --unclean` on a `memory` group restarts every fence table it held above every token `#locks` has handed out (OPS-07's rule for a restore); then E-24's lock and saga bounds run with a group that can lose its unsynced tail, once without the rule and once with it. Rows with Q `maj-d` keep met: there a committed raise is lost only with a majority's disks, F-12's operator case, as RR-11 ruled.

cells.by: referee for VERDICT draft 3's re-rule list (VERDICT.md section 11.3, items 1 to 7), 2026-11-11
cells.why: Open, not met, for the same lost tail. These two rows hold Q `mix` and D `sess`. A session's outcomes and floor, and a refusal that waited for its commit (A-04), sit in the same group's log as the writes, so a `memory` group whose majority stops uncleanly loses them with its unsynced tail. E-20's model lets a copy of an attempt reach a group at any time, and it holds 'a refused attempt never commits later' because the refusal is kept. With the refusal in the lost tail, a late copy of the same attempt is judged again after `fero recover --unclean` and can commit: a copy that a forwarder still holds, or a keyed method re-run, which issues the same attempt ids (E-20, 'Keyed calls'). Then an attempt told 'refused' commits later, which F-02 forbids. A fence refusal goes back the same way (RR-12). The met cell's support leaves this out in its own words: E-20's groups are crash-only ('Unclean recovery (a committed log cut back)' is left out), E-32 left the rung out ('the unsynced tail a `memory` rung can lose is not modelled'), and E-30's groups are crash-only. AMENDMENTS 4 lists 'session floors' in K-09's unsynced tail. Not fails: reasoned, not run, and no second agent confirmed a structural argument. Closer: either session-bound writes, refusals and fence raises never sit on a `memory` resource, or `fero recover --unclean` on a `memory` group starts a new session generation for its slots, as a restore does (A-08, E-33: a retry from an older generation is refused); then E-20's bounds run with a lost tail. DRAFT and SPLIT, the other rows with the rung, are open already (RR-05). Rows with Q `maj-d` keep met.

cells.why: The cell stays open; RR-11's closer narrows to its refusal half for these rows as they stand. RR-11 named two ways to close P-15: a saga's steps, fence raises and end record on a `memory` resource commit at `persisted` ('Q `mix` may choose per write'), or the saga library refuses such a unit. The first needs a rung chosen per write, and none of these rows has one. COMP's definition forbids it: AMENDMENTS 4, footnote 13, '`maj-m` and `none` per resource, never per write, because G `pslot` cuts groups by durability'. COMP2's family shares that footnote. DRAFT, CELL and SPLIT set the rung per resource in their own sources (DESIGN-V5 3.2: '`durability` has two rungs, per resource', and decision 4b; V5-PRIMITIVE: the rungs are parameters of a cell; V5-UNITS: per-resource durability). SPACE's Q `mix` allows a per-write choice, so for those three shard rows it would be a change of the row (a second rung inside one group, v4's ladder), not a rule they hold; for the `pslot` rows it is ruled out. So the closer these rows can state is the refusal: no saga step, fence raise or end record on a `memory` resource. With RR-12's and RR-13's closers it is one rule: locks, fences, sagas and session-bound writes never sit on a `memory` resource. Its model run is RR-11's (E-24 with a lost tail, without and with the rule). This narrows what P-15 offers a `memory` resource; it moves no cell.

cells.by: referee for VERDICT draft 3's re-rule list (VERDICT.md section 11.3, items 1 to 7), 2026-11-11
cells.why: The fail stands; its gap is 0.07, not 0.39. Rule 2 asks for the distance the proof shows, and RR-04 itself refused a gap counted from a figure that is not the row's floor. Its 0.422 ms adds the round trip's p99 (58 us) as a constant, twice, and a p99 added as a constant is not a lower bound, so 0.39 claims more than is shown. Recomputed here from the same table (E-01's one-writer fdatasync quantiles, 290,235 samples), with three independent disks: the second-fastest of three fsyncs has p99 0.323 ms with no network cost at all (gap 0.066). Counting the client's hop by a bound that holds for any shape of round-trip time (for independent parts, P(X + Y > a + b) is at least P(X > a) times P(Y > b), so the p99 of the sum is at least the race's p98, 0.295 ms, plus the hop's median, 30.6 us in Rust), it is at least 0.326 ms (gap 0.075). Both round to 0.07, and both are above the 0.303 ms bar, so no `persisted` commit on this box can win JetStream's default row: the fail holds. The figures in between (0.23 with the median round trip added as a constant; 0.39 with its p99) estimate a real commit; they are not bounds. Effect: each of these rows' gap sum falls by 0.32 (1.71 to 1.39 where the row fails SC-03, SC-10 and PERF-04). As worded, PD (6 MUSTs failed, 1.39) now ranks above CELL (6, 1.54); no winner moves. The alternative and its dependence stay: open if the user accepts JetStream's default row as a loss by name.

cells.by: referee for VERDICT draft 3's re-rule list (VERDICT.md section 11.3, items 1 to 7), 2026-11-11
cells.why: The cell stays open; its reason changes. The settled reason calls Rust's 0.33 ms 'a win' and says 'the native step carries' JetStream's default row. That was written against JetStream's 0.55 ms, before RR-04 set the win bar by PERF-01's spread rule at about 0.303 ms p99 (0.550 ms, over runs of 0.536 to 0.783 ms, E-09b). Against that bar neither of E-02's `memory` figures wins: 0.57 ms in TypeScript, 0.33 ms in Rust. So no measurement shows any rung winning the default row. Nor is a loss shown: E-02 read both at 50,000 writes a second with no client hop and no gateway, never with one write in flight, and one working point is no ceiling (RR-02, RR-03 for P-05). cells.why: The strict reading stays as RR-10 framed it, now written out; SRV's and PD's cells do not change; COMP2's pin is accepted. (1) Written out: on the strict reading, data's own code folds every row of record (the rows a replica serves, reads, replays and judges writes by) on writers and followers, in every phase the row plans. A row fails it by structure when its own tags put those rows in another engine: servers that fold in Rust or Go (F `all(srv)`: SRV), or a kernel whose commands write the rows into its own store (K `kern` with an LSM: PD's multi-version store, in Rust or in TypeScript). Those are the two cases RR-10's referee named, and the tool encodes exactly them. (2) Rows whose tags leave the fold to a design rule are not failed by it: a `ts→rs` row's native step (both DATA-09 judges, for every such row: 'the row either keeps data folding in JavaScript ... or holds rows natively'), an H `srv` row after its Rust core (its server can keep a Node host for data), a kernel worker's compact copy of the rows (M `kw`, A-27), and K `lib` with an LSM that stores data's rows. DESIGN-V5 plans a Rust L0 to L3 and a kernel that owns the rows, so the evidence skeptic (F1) showed that a word-for-word reading of that plan would fail most rows. But the DATA-09 judges read the native step as undecided, RR-10 framed the reading for SRV and PD only, and a structural fail needs a second agent's written confirmation, which no one has given for these rows. So their cells stay as they are. Such a row passes the strict reading for sure only by stating that data keeps folding (REQUIREMENTS X3's first way), and any of them may state it. (3) COMP2's pin is a design rule the row may carry. It is recorded as part of the definition of COMP2 and of the six family A rows that share its plan (hybrids/A.settled.json, 'pins'), not SRV V=full Y=fwd, whose tags fold natively. The pin: the native core holds L0 and L1 and never folds rows; L2 and data's fold stay in JavaScript, as RUST's row has them (A-30's call rules; E-03: under 1 ns a record at batch 256); every full replica keeps a full data projection; and the kernel worker keeps at most an index or cache of the rows (A-27), never served and checked against data's rows by F-21's hash (E-05: the two digests matched). Its price is memory: E-05 put both copies at 510 to 528 B a small row, under DEP-13's 2 KB, and E-34 woke 5.1 GB of 2 KB rows in that form, but at 10 GB it needs about twice the heap and could not run on the 16 GB box; SC-05 is open on its own reasons either way, and an index without the values halves the cost. It adds no mechanism and moves no rule-3 count. It meets DATA-09 by construction, for the reason both judges gave RUST's met cell ('data's own JS code still folds, so the fold's results are data's by identity'). DATA-01 stays open on its settled reasons (E-22's one thread, E-23's merge contract, E-05's digest only). If a later timing shows L2 must go native, the row drops the pin, DATA-09 goes back to open, and on the strict reading the row then fails as SRV does. (4) TiKV-persisted failed through SRV's rule (F `all(srv)`) and carried SRV's reason, though its engine is PD's. PD's rule now comes first, so it carries PD's reason. Its verdict does not move. Effect: COMP2's open MUSTs fall by one (DATA-09); no matrix winner moves.

cells.why: TiKV-TS (a closure row, so no study row is listed): kept open on the loose reading and failing on the strict one, as now. The reason is restated and the row takes a pin. In its TypeScript phase its servers keep MVCC versions in an LSM written in TypeScript by kernel commands (K `kern`, S `lsm +tier`, L `ts→rs`): neither data's lane nor native code. So the borrowed reason ('rows whose servers fold natively') is wrong for that phase. The verdict is not. The loose reading, as the judges and RR-07 read it, lets a server fold in another engine once a differential test proves its rows equal data's fold ('PD meets DATA-01 only if a differential test proves that store's rows equal data's fold'). What makes another engine acceptable there is the proof of equal rows, not the language. DATA-09's words ('if any layer moves to native code') say when that test is owed, not which engines it may clear, and nothing in the files reads them as clearing a native engine but not a TypeScript one. A fail on the loose reading would need a structural argument a second agent confirms in writing: the independent skeptic (I-2) called it plausible and left it to a referee, and no second agent confirmed it. So the cell stands: open on the loose reading; fails by structure on the strict reading and on the middle one (a TypeScript MVCC store is neither data's lane nor a port of it). The pin, recorded in hybrids/B.settled.json (B1): DATA-09's differential test against data binds the servers' store from the TypeScript phase on, not only after the native step, because that test is the only path by which this row meets DATA-01 on the loose reading, and DATA-09's words alone would not oblige it before the native step. It adds no mechanism and moves no count; DATA-09 stays open (the test was not run). The loose leader does not move: TiKV-TS, tied by its native twin (PD+fix Y=fwd M=kw Z=par), whose cell has the same verdict on its own reason.
